metadata.title: Claude, Recalibrated
metadata.subtitle: Professor Bear's notes on Ranfei's Visa-Risk Runway Engine
metadata.framing: Liam asks Claude what feedback Professor Bear would give the student. FIRST NAME ONLY — 'Ranfei', 'Professor Bear' / 'Bear'. Never the student's surname.
metadata.one_idea: Generalizing a working pipeline isn't adding rows — each new scope silently breaks an assumption the original was calibrated on; the skeptic re-derives confidence, thresholds, and the risk-clock for the new scope instead of porting them.

beats.narration_text: Sawadee — this is Liam, in for Bear. Ranfei wants to generalize a working visa-risk pipeline: widen it past FAANG, and add the STEM OPT extension clock. I asked Claude what Professor Bear would say. Short version — that's two changes, each quietly breaking an assumption. Re-derive them. Don't port them.

props.command: What feedback would Professor Bear give Ranfei on generalizing the Visa-Risk Runway Engine — FAANG — a broad company pool, plus STEM OPT extension timing?

beats.narration_text: First, why this is two projects.

Both moves sound like natural scope expansion — add more companies, add another deadline. That's the trap. Each one quietly breaks an assumption the original five-step pipeline was calibrated on, and doing both at once makes it easy to miss that they interact.

props.title: One Move, Two Broken Assumptions
props.note: each scope change cracks a different calibrated assumption
branches: Initial OPT / STEM extension: clock structure breaks

beats.show: A single 'generalize' arrow forks into two arrows that each crack a labeled assumption.

beats.narration_text: So treat it as two engineering problems that happen to share a codebase. One: widening the company pool. Two: the extension clock. Bear's told Ranfei to build them as two problems, because the shortcut — one generalization — is where the skepticism gets skipped.
beats.show: One box splits into two labeled tracks: 'Widen the pool' and 'The extension clock', running in parallel.

beats.narration_text: Now the first assumption that breaks.

Widening the pool isn't 'add more rows' — it's a data-confidence problem. Every signal degrades differently off FAANG. The killer: at a Series B startup, 'no H-1B filing history' isn't 'confirmed non-sponsor.' It's an absence of data. Score both toward RED and you systematically bury real jobs at growing companies.
beats.show: A single 'signal' splits into two axes — VALUE and CONFIDENCE — that had been collapsed into one bar.

beats.narration_text: Picture the company that loses most from this bug — a forty-person startup that would sponsor, but has never filed because it's never had to. The tool the student built to surface hidden opportunities would be the tool that hides it.
beats.show: A small startup office, a few desks — the kind of company with no filing history yet. Slow push in.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a small early-stage startup workspace, documentary duotone.

beats.narration_text: So the fix is to make confidence a first-class output. Ask for this:

props.command: Write sponsorship_signal(company) that separates signal VALUE from CONFIDENCE — a thin-data startup must never silently inherit a FAANG-calibrated RED.

beats.narration_text: Value and confidence, side by side. Zero filings at a startup returns 'unknown, low confidence' — a note, not a verdict. Zero filings at a FAANG returns 'non-sponsor, high confidence,' because there, absence is informative. Same input, two epistemic states.

props.title: sponsorship_signal.py

beats.show: Onda code-block types sponsorship_signal(...); the two zero-filing branches highlight in turn.

beats.narration_text: Then the RED-AMBER-GREEN call becomes a function of both value and confidence — not value alone. An 'unknown, low-confidence' startup must render differently than a 'confirmed non-sponsor, high-confidence' FAANG, even when a naive pipeline would score them identically.
beats.show: Two companies with identical color land in different cells of a value×confidence grid.

beats.narration_text: Now the second assumption — and it's a bigger one.

The STEM OPT extension isn't the initial-OPT deadline shifted later. It's a structurally different risk model — a terminal window, with no extension after it. Port the April-lottery logic and just move the date, and you've modeled the wrong machine. It's two coupled clocks, each with its own lottery cycle.
beats.show: One deadline timeline splits into two distinct state machines running side by side, the second ending in a hard STOP.

beats.narration_text: And the terminal clock keeps running during adjudication. The 180-day automatic extension while STEM OPT is pending is work-authorized — but it still counts against the 24-month total…
beats.show: A 24-month runway bar; a 'pending adjudication' segment eats into it rather than pausing it. Camera holds.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a depleting runway/hourglass motif; continuity into B10 (vox_run R1).

beats.narration_text: …so the runway erodes even when everything's filed correctly, and when it closes, there's no fallback. That terminal moment is the highest-stakes point in a student's whole OPT lifecycle — it has to outrank the initial deadline, not sit as a second row of the same kind.
beats.show: Continuous move from the eroding bar to the hard STOP at its end, flagged 'terminal — no fallback'.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: the runway ending at a wall/stop; continuity from B09.

beats.narration_text: So model two clocks, not one shifted deadline. Ask for this:

props.command: Model initial-OPT and STEM-extension as two coupled but distinct clocks, each gated by its own lottery cycle and cap-gap rule; flag the STEM window terminal.

beats.narration_text: Two windows, each with its own lottery attempts and cap-gap rule. And note the cap-gap comment — the rule changed. Recently it can run to about April first of the next year, not stop at September thirtieth. A model still hard-coding the old September stop is running stale logic — verify it against current guidance.

props.title: compute_risk_windows.py
props.code:
def compute_risk_windows(student):
    windows = []
    initial_end = student.opt_start + timedelta(days=365)
    windows.append({'phase': 'initial_opt', 'hard_deadline': initial_end,
        'lottery_attempts_remaining': 2 if student.stem_eligible else 1,
        'cap_gap_extension_to': 'April 1 of following FY (verify vs current USCIS guidance)'})
    if student.stem_eligible:
        stem_end = initial_end + timedelta(days=730)
        windows.append({'phase': 'stem_extension', 'hard_deadline': stem_end,
            'lottery_attempts_remaining': 1, 'terminal': True,
            'note': 'Adjudication delays still consume this 24-month total'})
    return windows

beats.show: Onda code-block types compute_risk_windows(...); the cap-gap line and the terminal flag highlight terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Which brings us to the thresholds.

If the GREEN cutoff — say, three filings in two years — was tuned by eyeballing FAANG data, applying it unchanged to startups misclassifies by default. A threshold is only as good as the population it came from. So show the distribution of raw signal values inside the NEW pool first, then draw the cutoff.
beats.show: A FAANG-tuned cutoff line drops onto a startup distribution and mislabels a cluster; the line then re-fits to the new histogram.

beats.narration_text: Robustness, aimed at exactly these two changes.

Four tests that target the generalization, not generic sensitivity. Tier-stratified: same raw inputs, FAANG versus startup — does the color change for the right reason? Regulatory-version: does the model tell the old September rule from the current April one? Sparse-data: does zero history render 'unknown', not RED? Terminal-primacy: does the STEM deadline outrank the initial one when both are close?
beats.show: Four test chips resolve: Tier-stratified · Regulatory-version · Sparse-data · Terminal-primacy.

beats.narration_text: The regulatory-version test is the one to insist on. Feed it a case where the old September stop and the current April date give different classifications. If the pipeline can't tell them apart, it's silently running a rule that no longer exists — the exact stale-assumption bug this course teaches you to hunt.
beats.show: A still of two calendars — Sept 30 vs April 1; a terracotta X draws through the outdated one.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: two calendar pages, one struck through; ring/X annotation at previz.

beats.narration_text: Last — the picture the student ships.

The FAANG-only version could get away with a clean three-color light, because the data was dense. The generalized one can't — not without misleading students at exactly the startups where the tool is most useful. Confirmed RED and unknown-low-confidence must not look the same, even when they score the same.
beats.show: Two identical red dots separate: one solid 'confirmed', one hatched 'unknown / low-confidence'.

beats.narration_text: And show which clock is binding — a student should see instantly whether the initial-OPT or the STEM-extension window is the constraint driving the color. Flag anything resting on an unverified regulatory assumption. The whole point of the tool is to help someone trust or distrust a recommendation — not just receive one.

lines: reg assumption: cap-gap rule — verify current USCIS guidance

beats.show: A risk card surfaces a 'binding: STEM-extension (terminal)' tag and a small 'reg assumption: verify' flag.

beats.narration_text: Under all five parts, one idea: generalizing isn't extending — it's recalibrating. The confidence dimension and the terminal clock are the load-bearing skepticism here, and they're the same moves that made Ranfei's own Reallocation Engine reliable in its narrow scope. Point at the open questions — how to weight startup equity, how to handle a student who hasn't entered either lottery — and let the wrestling be the assignment.
beats.show: Two tracks ('pool' and 'clock') converge on a single label: 'Recalibrate, don't extend.'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Bear's notes for Ranfei, in five. Widening the pool is a data-confidence problem — 'no history' is not 'non-sponsor.' The STEM extension is a different, terminal clock, not a later deadline — and verify the cap-gap rule, it changed. Re-derive the thresholds on the new pool; don't port FAANG cutoffs. Test the two generalizations directly. And make the picture show confidence and the binding clock. Strong extension of real work — now recalibrate it instead of extending it.

artifactLines: Widen the pool = data-confidence, not coverage: no history ≠ non-sponsor
STEM extension = a separate TERMINAL clock; verify the cap-gap rule (it changed)
Adjudication delays consume the 24-month total — they don't pause it
Re-derive thresholds on the new pool; don't port FAANG cutoffs
Visualize confidence + which clock is binding, not just the color

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude on any model you're widening to a new population. It forces you to split value from confidence, catch every ported threshold, version-test the assumptions that changed, and find where the picture hides doubt — then it leaves you two open questions instead of answers. Run it before you call your generalization done, and watch what it refuses to let you carry over.

props.command: I'm generalizing a risk classifier that was calibrated on one narrow population to a much broader one. Pressure-test it: (1) for each input signal, force me to separate its VALUE from my CONFIDENCE in it for the new population, and flag any 'missing data' I'm scoring as a real negative; (2) find any threshold I ported from the old population instead of re-deriving on the new one, and make me show the new distribution; (3) find any time/deadline/regulatory assumption that changed and make me add a version test; (4) tell me where the visualization hides uncertainty. End with two open questions I have to answer myself.

beats.narration_text: Claude, Recalibrated.
